extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants / practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: patent prosecution timing and special status
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on requesting and handling 'special' status petitions, suspensions, shortened statutory periods, extensions of time, and computing reply periods during patent prosecution. Also covers procedural handling and recording of petitions and examiner duties related to these timing matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews after a final Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal interview after a final Office action will not be permitted unless requested by the examiner. Telephonic interviews will be permitted where appropriate for the purpose of correcting any minor outstanding matters. Telephone may be used to inform the applicant of relatively minor issues or deficiencies that might be easily resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of telephone or telephonic interviews is limited to minor issues and is not intended to open the door to further prosecution after a final action. Examiners may use telephone when appropriate to correct minor outstanding matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special status for superconductivity applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO will, on request, accord 'special' status to all patent applications for inventions involving superconductivity materials. Requests should be accompanied by a statement under 37 CFR 1.102 that the invention involves superconductive materials. No fee is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include inventions directed to superconductive materials themselves and to their manufacture and application. Applicants seeking participation should request special status and include the 37 CFR 1.102 statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special status for HIV/AIDS and cancer applications
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO will accord 'special' status to patent applications relating to HIV/AIDS and cancer. Applicants desiring special status should file a petition and the fee under 37 CFR 1.17(i) requesting special status, accompanied by a statement explaining how the invention contributes to the diagnosis, treatment or prevention of HIV/AIDS or cancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the public health importance, petitions must explain the contribution of the invention to diagnosis, treatment or prevention. The petition and required fee are necessary for these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special status for counter-terrorism inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO will accord 'special' status to patent applications relating to counter-terrorism inventions. Applicants should file a petition with the petition fee under 37 CFR 1.17(i) requesting special status, accompanied by a statement explaining how the invention contributes to countering terrorism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International terrorism is defined (18 U.S.C. 2331); example technologies include systems for detecting/identifying explosives, aircraft sensors/security systems, and vehicular barricades/disabling systems. Petition must explain the contribution to countering terrorism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special status for biotechnology applications filed by small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who are small entities may request that their biotechnology applications be granted 'special' status by filing a petition with the petition fee under 37 CFR 1.17(i). The applicant must (A) state that small entity status has been established or include a statement establishing small entity status; (B) state that the subject of the patent application is a major asset of the small entity; and (C) state that development of the technology will be significantly impaired if examination is delayed, including an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three showings (small entity, major asset, significant impairment with explanation) are required to justify special handling for small-entity-filed biotech applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements of a petition to make special
rubrics_metrics.description: Any petition to make special should be in writing and identify the application by application number and filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions lacking these formalities may not be properly processed; include identification information to allow correct file entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and recording of petitions to make special
rubrics_metrics.description: Each petition to make special, regardless of ground, is made of record in the application file together with the decision thereon. The petition and any attached papers will be given a single paper number and entered in the 'Contents' of the file; the decision will be accorded a separate paper number. The part of the Office that rules on a petition is responsible for entering the petition and decision in the file record. Petitions to make special are decided by the Special Program Examiner of the patent examining group to which the application is assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical support staff in the examining group must ensure proper ordering of 'Contents' and that all papers prior to a petition are entered/listed before forwarding for petition consideration. Applications made special are advanced out of turn and treated as special throughout prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of action — grounds and general rule (37 CFR 1.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension of action by the Office will be granted for good and sufficient cause and for a reasonable time specified upon petition by the applicant and, if such cause is not the fault of the Office, the payment of the fee set forth in § 1.17(i). Action will not be suspended when a reply by applicant to an Office action is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension applies to impending Office action by the examiner (not to applicant's reply). If requirements of 37 CFR 1.103 are not met, the application will be taken up in order. If the Office suspends action sua sponte, §1.103(b) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition requirements for suspension of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for suspension of action must be presented as a separate paper accompanied by the petition fee, must request a specific and reasonable period of suspension not greater than 6 months, and must present good and sufficient reasons why the suspension is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximum period for any suspension is six months. The primary examiner may grant an initial suspension for up to 6 months; any second or subsequent suspension must be approved by the Group Director. Certain suspensions (e.g., under 37 CFR 1.103(c)) are decided by the Director of Group 3640.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of action is distinct from extension of time for reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension of action (37 CFR 1.103) applies to impending Office action by the examiner, whereas extension of time for reply (37 CFR 1.136) applies to action by the applicant. Action cannot be suspended in an application which contains an outstanding Office action or requirement awaiting reply by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and examiners should not confuse the two procedural devices; they have different purposes, procedures, and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitions to suspend action to allow IDS are denied
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for suspension of action to allow applicant time to submit an information disclosure statement will be denied as failing to present good and sufficient reasons, since 37 CFR 1.97 provides adequate recourse for the timely submission of prior art for consideration by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should use the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97/1.98 for IDS submission rather than seeking suspension under 1.103 for that purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for suspension of action (¶ 7.52–7.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard Office action paragraphs should be used for suspension matters, e.g., ¶7.52 Suspension of Action, Awaiting New Reference; ¶7.53 Suspension of Action, Possible Interference; ¶7.54 Suspension of Action, Applicant's Request; ¶7.56 Request for Suspension, Denied, Outstanding Office Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs include examiner notes such as maximum period (6 months) and reminders that Group Director must approve second or subsequent suspensions. They provide standard language and procedural reminders to ensure consistent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment for failure to reply (37 CFR 1.135)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant of a patent application fails to reply within the time period provided under § 1.134 and § 1.136, the application will become abandoned unless an Office action indicates otherwise. Prosecution to save an application from abandonment must include such complete and proper reply as the condition of the application may require. The admission of, or refusal to admit, any amendment after final rejection or any amendment not responsive to the last action will not operate to save the application from abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must file timely, complete, and proper replies. Certain late or nonresponsive amendments do not avoid abandonment. See 37 CFR 1.135 for exceptions and nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for inadvertent omissions in replies (37 CFR 1.135(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: When reply by the applicant is a bona fide attempt to advance the application and is substantially a complete reply to the non-final Office action but includes an inadvertent omission, the examiner may consider that reply adequate to avoid abandonment and give the applicant a shortened statutory time period (generally 1 month) to correct the omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of omissions that may be cured within the 1-month period include unsigned papers, improperly signed papers, missing duplicate papers, or missing fees for additional claims. The examiner has discretion; if the omission was not inadvertent (e.g., apparent abuse to gain time), the examiner may require correction within the prior period and deny the 1-month cure. If the omission does not preclude action on the merits, the examiner may waive the deficiency and act on the reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of statutory periods for reply (how computed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual time taken for reply is computed from the date stamped or printed on the Office action to the date of receipt by the Office of applicant's reply. No cognizance is taken of fractions of a day and applicant's reply is due on the corresponding day of the month 6 months or any lesser number specified after the Office action. A 30-day period means 30 calendar days (including weekends and Federal holidays) but if the period ends on a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, the reply is timely if filed on the next succeeding business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate corresponding-day computation (e.g., Nov 30 → Feb 28). A 1-month extension extends to the corresponding date next month. The Office date stamp determines receipt date. Where the statutory reply period runs from the date of a previous action, the Office action should state that fact explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of time — general rule (37 CFR 1.136(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant is required to reply within a nonstatutory or shortened statutory time period, applicant may extend the time period for reply up to the earlier of the expiration of any maximum period set by statute or five months after the time period set for reply, if a petition for an extension of time and the fee set in § 1.17(a) are filed, unless: (i) Applicant is notified otherwise in an Office action; (ii) The reply is a reply brief under § 1.193(b); (iii) The reply is a request for an oral hearing under § 1.194(b); (iv) The reply is to a Board decision under §§ 1.196, 1.197 or 1.304; or (v) The application is involved in an interference declared under § 1.611.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date the petition and fee are filed determines the period and fee. A reply must be filed prior to expiration of the extension to avoid abandonment. See §1.136(b) for other extension situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive petitions for extension of time
rubrics_metrics.description: A written request may be submitted authorizing treatment of any concurrent or future reply that would require a petition for extension of time as incorporating a petition for extension of time; authorization to charge required fees or submission of the fee will be treated as a constructive petition for extension for concurrent or future replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows applicants to pre-authorize charging fees so that future replies requiring extension are treated as if a petition were filed on the date of authorization/fee submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of time when 37 CFR 1.136(a) not available (37 CFR 1.136(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reply cannot be filed within the time period set for such reply and the provisions of paragraph (a) are not available, the period for reply will be extended only for sufficient cause and for a reasonable time specified. Any request under this paragraph must be filed on or before the day the reply is due; mere filing does not effect an extension. No extension can carry the due date beyond the maximum time period set by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (b) is narrower and requires sufficient cause; it cannot be used to exceed statutory maxima. See related rules for appeals, interferences, reexamination, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations using shortened statutory periods (specific periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortened statutory periods are used depending on the type of reply required and may not be less than 30 days. Examples provided: 1-month (not less than 30 days) for requirement for restriction/election of species only, or for correcting an inadvertent omission; 2 months for Ex parte Quayle actions or for winning party in terminated interference to reply to an unanswered Office action; 3 months to reply to any Office action on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner has directed examiners to set a shortened period for every action; the appropriate length depends on what reply is required. Special situations may change the periods under rare circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified time limits (non-statutory) and their consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are situations where the examiner specifies a time for the applicant to take an action and the failure to timely take that specified action results in consequences other than abandonment. Examples: (A) Petition for public access under 37 CFR 1.14(e): applicant usually given 3 weeks to state objections — failure results in PTO decision without applicant's objections; (B) Incomplete information disclosure statement: examiner may set a 1-month time limit to complete IDS — failure results in noncomplying info placed in file but not considered; (C) When application is otherwise allowable but contains traverse of restriction requirement: applicant may be given e.g., 1-month to cancel claims to nonelected invention — failure treated as authorization to cancel and application passed to issue; (D) Suggested claims for interference must be presented within at least one month or be treated as a disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified time limits can be less than 30 days and do not cause abandonment if missed; instead they cause loss of rights in the specific matter (e.g., disclaimer, non-consideration of incomplete IDS contents). Examiners may set such limits where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between shortened statutory periods and specified time limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to reply within a shortened statutory period under 35 U.S.C. 133 results in abandonment of the entire application and is not appealable (though revival petitions may be available under 37 CFR 1.137). In contrast, failure to meet a specified time for a particular action results in loss of rights only regarding that particular matter and does not necessarily cause abandonment. Also, specified time limits are not subject to the 30-day minimum and may be less than 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and applicants must recognize this distinction because the consequences differ greatly. A reply 1–2 days late under a specified time might be excused, while any lateness under a statutory shortened period results in abandonment (subject to revival rules).
